big_case_rationale: A clean statutory circuit split with real stakes for terminated asylees and their derivative spouses and children, sharpened by the current wave of asylum terminations, but technical adjustment-of-status doctrine rather than a headline constitutional or structural question.

semantic_claims.proposition: The majority holds that the phrase 'any alien granted asylum' in 8 U.S.C. § 1159(b)'s prefatory clause denotes the completed past event of an asylum grant, not a continuing present status, adopting the Fifth Circuit's Siwe reading and rejecting the 'status signals a present condition' inference of Cela and the Second Circuit. The holding rests on intra-section contrast: Congress wrote express continuing-status requirements three times in § 1159 — § 1159(a)(1)(A) ('has not been terminated'), (b)(3) ('continues to be a refugee'), and (b)(5) (admissible 'at the time of examination') — so its omission of any continuing-asylum requirement from (b)'s prefatory clause is treated as deliberate, with § 1159(b)(2)'s 'after being granted asylum' confirming the past-event usage. The judgment rests on text and structure, not on the immigration lenity canon and not on deference to the DOJ regulation.

The majority states a categorical rule rather than a fact-bound one: every noncitizen once granted asylum remains statutorily eligible for § 1159(b) adjustment regardless of why or when the asylum was later terminated — criminal-conviction terminations like petitioners' included — with the safeguard against undeserving applicants located in § 1159(b)(3) and (b)(5)'s express criteria and the Attorney General's retained case-by-case discretion to deny adjustment, not in a threshold eligibility bar. The opinion does not confine the holding to no-fault terminations, to derivative asylees, or to these petitioners.
